definition: An emergent algorithm is an algorithm that exhibits emergent behavior.
details: In essence an emergent algorithm implements a set of simple building block behaviors that when combined exhibit more complex behaviors. One example of this is the implementation of fuzzy motion controllers used to adapt robot movement in response to environmental obstacles. An emergent algorithm has the following characteristics: it achieves predictable global effects it does not require global visibility it does not assume any kind of centralized control it is self-stabilizing Other examples of emergent algorithms and models include cellular automata, artificial neural networks and swarm intelligence systems (ant colony optimization, bees algorithm, etc.).

explainer.lead: An emergent algorithm combines simple behaviors so that their interactions produce a more complex, predictable result. It matters because this can be achieved without giving any component a complete view of the system or putting a central controller in charge.

tiers.eli5: Imagine several dancers who each follow a few simple instructions based only on the people nearby. Together, their movements can form a coordinated pattern even though nobody is directing the whole group. An emergent algorithm works similarly: small actions combine into a bigger, useful behavior.
tiers.practitioner: Apply this approach by designing simple local behaviors and evaluating the predictable global effect produced by their interactions. Examples include fuzzy motion controllers for obstacle-responsive robots, ant colony optimization, and the bees algorithm. A key pitfall is introducing global visibility or centralized coordination, while another is failing to check that the combined system remains self-stabilizing.
tiers.paperLevel: Let component i update its local state and action using a rule f_i(s_i, o_i), where s_i is local state and o_i contains only locally available observations. The algorithm is emergent when the interaction of these simple rules yields predictable, more complex global behavior without global visibility or centralized control, and the system is self-stabilizing. Cellular automata, artificial neural networks, and swarm intelligence systems provide other examples of emergent algorithms and models.

explainer.example: A robot's fuzzy motion controller can combine a forward-moving behavior with simple responses to nearby environmental obstacles. When an obstacle is detected locally, the obstacle response changes the movement command; combined with the other behaviors, this produces adaptive obstacle-avoiding motion without one component seeing the whole environment.

explainer.goal: Produce a predictable, complex global effect by combining simple component behaviors, without requiring global visibility or centralized control, while remaining self-stabilizing.
inputs: Environmental conditions such as nearby obstacles
steps: Define a set of simple building-block behaviors.
Let each component act using the information available to it, without requiring global visibility.
Combine the components' actions without assuming centralized control.
Allow their interactions to produce the more complex global behavior.
Check that the global effect is predictable and that the system is self-stabilizing.
tradeoffs: No component needs a complete view of the environment.
The combined behavior is more complex than its simple building blocks.
Predictable global effects must still be established.
Self-stabilization is a required property, not an automatic consequence of using local rules.
